context: Cover letters go to strangers with hiring power -- they need full words, no slang, courteous distance. The other three are for close family or the household. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.220.

question: A coworker leans over a desk and says, 'Hey, wanna grab lunch?' Which register does that sentence use?
answer: Casual
choices: Casual
Formal
Academic
Technical
context: Contractions ('wanna'), slang ('grab'), short, informal address ('hey') -- the mark of the casual register used in texts and chats between friends. Source: Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage, entry 'register'.

question: A job seeker's letter begins, 'Dear Ms. Smith, I would like to inquire about the position advertised on Monday.' Which register does that sentence use?
answer: Formal
choices: Formal
Casual
Technical
Literary
context: Full words (no contractions), courteous distance ('Dear Ms. Smith'), no slang. Used in business letters, job applications, formal invitations. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.220.

question: A sleep researcher begins her report, 'This paper examines the relationship between sleep and short-term memory in seventh-graders.' Which register does that sentence use?
answer: Academic
choices: Academic
Casual
Technical
Literary
context: Third-person voice, precise vocabulary, a signal that sources will be cited. That is the essay-and-research-paper register. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.220.

question: A programmer's bug log reads, 'The debugger traces a segmentation fault to line 47.' Which register does that sentence use?
answer: Technical
choices: Technical
Academic
Formal
Casual
context: 'Debugger,' 'segmentation fault,' 'line 47' -- specialized vocabulary for a specific field (programming). A segmentation fault is a crash while a program runs, so the debugger finds it, not the compiler. Technical register is used in manuals, specifications, and engineering documents.

question: Carl Sandburg wrote in 1916, 'The fog comes on little cat feet.' Which register does that line use?
answer: Literary
choices: Literary
Academic
Technical
Formal
context: The comparison of fog to a cat is imagery, not report. Sandburg's 'Fog' (1916) is the classroom-standard example of the literary register. Source: Grokipedia 'Register (sociolinguistics)' (2026-09-05).

question: A student opens a school research paper with 'So basically what this paper's gonna be about is how kids sleep matters a bunch for memory and stuff.' What is the main problem?
answer: The register is casual -- slang like 'gonna' does not suit an essay
choices: The register is casual -- slang like 'gonna' does not suit an essay
The voice is passive -- the opener hides who did the study
The sentence is a fragment -- it never reaches a main verb
The tense is wrong -- a research paper must use the past tense
context: 'Basically,' 'gonna,' 'kids,' 'a bunch,' 'and stuff' are the casual register. An academic essay needs precise vocabulary and third-person voice. The sentence is not passive, it has a main verb ('is'), and no rule forces a research paper into the past tense.

question: A yearbook caption reads, 'She is one of the students who ___ hard.' Which verb form does the traditional rule call for?
answer: work
choices: work
works
has worked
is working
context: The traditional rule: the verb inside the relative clause agrees with the noun the relative pronoun refers to. 'Who' -> 'students' (plural) -> 'work'. Chicago keeps this rule; Merriam-Webster's usage dictionary also allows a singular verb when the writer is thinking of the one person.

question: A principal's award letter reads, 'She is the only one of the students who ___ hard.' Which verb form fits?
answer: works
choices: works
work
have worked
are working
context: 'THE ONLY ONE' shifts the relative reference to 'one' (singular). Compare 'one of the students who work' (plural) vs 'the only one of the students who works' (singular). Chicago 5.66.

question: A boy leaves a note for his sister: 'The book that ___ on the table is mine.' Which verb fits?
answer: is
choices: is
are
were
sit
context: The relative pronoun THAT refers to its antecedent BOOK (singular). Verb agrees with BOOK → 'is'. Not with any other noun in the sentence.

question: A shop owner's inventory report reads, 'The list of items that ___ missing is long.' Which verb fits?
answer: are -- agrees with 'items'
choices: are -- agrees with 'items'
is -- agrees with 'list'
is -- agrees with 'items'
are -- agrees with 'list'
context: 'That' refers to ITEMS (plural), so verb inside the relative clause is 'are'. The main clause verb 'is' agrees with LIST (singular). Two separate agreements in one sentence.

question: A best man's toast begins, 'He is one of those people who ___ never late.' Which verb does the traditional rule call for?
answer: are
choices: are
is
was
seems
context: The classic 'one of those...who' construction. WHO refers to PEOPLE (plural), so the traditional rule wants a plural verb. 'One of those runners who never quit'; 'one of those songs that stay in a listener's head'.

question: An editor tries one line of a magazine profile four ways, each with a relative clause after 'writers.' Which version follows the traditional rule?
answer: She is one of the writers who work at night.
choices: She is one of the writers who work at night.
She is one of the writers who works at night.
She is one of the writers that works at night.
She is one of the writers who is working at night.
context: WHO refers to 'writers' (plural) -> 'work'. The traditional rule gives 'one of the X who' a plural verb because WHO refers to X, and THAT follows the same rule. 'The only one of the writers who works' would be singular.

question: A family's road-trip diary reads, 'A box of chocolates that ___ melting in the sun sat on the dashboard.' Which verb fits?
answer: were -- agrees with 'chocolates'
choices: were -- agrees with 'chocolates'
was -- agrees with 'box'
are -- agrees with 'chocolates'
is -- agrees with 'box'
context: 'That' inside the relative clause refers to CHOCOLATES (plural): the chocolates are what melt, so 'were melting'. The main clause verb 'sat' has 'box' (singular) as its subject. 'Are' and 'is' break the past tense the diary is told in. Two verbs, two different agreements.

question: A mail carrier drafts his report two ways: 'The dog that bit me ran off' and 'The dog, which bit me, ran off.' What signal does each version send the reader?
answer: No commas picks out one dog among several; commas add news about the only dog
choices: No commas picks out one dog among several; commas add news about the only dog
No commas adds news about the only dog; commas pick out one dog among several
The two versions mean exactly the same thing
The comma version is wrong, because 'which' cannot follow 'dog'
context: Without commas the clause identifies WHICH dog (restrictive, usually THAT). With commas it adds news about a dog already known (non-restrictive, WHICH in American usage).

question: An American copy editor reaches a restrictive clause, one that says which book is meant and cannot be cut without losing meaning. Which punctuation and pronoun does formal American writing prefer for it?
answer: 'The book that I read yesterday was great.' -- THAT, no commas
choices: 'The book that I read yesterday was great.' -- THAT, no commas
'The book, which I read yesterday, was great.' -- WHICH, with commas
'The book which I read yesterday was great.' -- WHICH, no commas
'The book, that I read yesterday was great.' -- THAT, one comma
context: American style (Chicago, AP) reserves THAT for restrictive and WHICH-with-commas for non-restrictive. British usage often uses WHICH for both. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.27.

question: A travel guide's draft leaves two gaps: 'Chicago ___ sits on Lake Michigan ___ has cold winters.' How should that sentence be punctuated?
answer: 'Chicago, which sits on Lake Michigan, has cold winters.' -- commas around WHICH clause
choices: 'Chicago, which sits on Lake Michigan, has cold winters.' -- commas around WHICH clause
'Chicago that sits on Lake Michigan has cold winters.' -- no commas, THAT
'Chicago which sits on Lake Michigan has cold winters.' -- no commas, WHICH
'Chicago; which sits on Lake Michigan; has cold winters.' -- semicolons
context: Chicago is a unique proper noun; the clause cannot RESTRICT it, only add info. Non-restrictive clauses with a unique noun always take commas and WHICH (in American usage). Source: Grokipedia 'English relative clauses' (2026-09-05).

question: A principal compares two drafts of a memo. One reads, 'The students who studied passed the test.' The other reads, 'The students, who studied, passed the test.' What difference in meaning do the commas create?
answer: No commas: only the students who studied passed. With commas: all the students studied, and all of them passed.
choices: No commas: only the students who studied passed. With commas: all the students studied, and all of them passed.
No commas: all the students studied and passed. With commas: only the ones who studied passed.
The two versions mean exactly the same thing.
The comma version is grammatically wrong.
context: Restrictive (no commas) filters -- 'the students who studied' is a subset. Non-restrictive (commas) adds info about ALL the students. Same sentence, two different worlds. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.27.

question: A driver drafts a complaint to his garage four ways. Which draft is punctuated correctly in American style?
answer: 'The car that I bought last week already has a flat tire.'
choices: 'The car that I bought last week already has a flat tire.'
'The car, that I bought last week, already has a flat tire.'
'The car, which I bought last week already has a flat tire.'
'The car; which I bought last week; already has a flat tire.'
context: The clause identifies WHICH car, so it is restrictive: THAT, no commas. THAT never takes commas around it, a clause opened with a comma must close with one, and semicolons cannot bracket a clause.

question: A hiker's logbook reads, 'The rain fell birds took shelter.' What error is this?
answer: run-on (fused) sentence
choices: run-on (fused) sentence
comma splice
fragment
misplaced modifier
context: RUN-ON (fused) SENTENCE: two independent clauses smashed together with NO punctuation or conjunction. A comma splice has a comma between them; a fragment is missing a part of a sentence; a misplaced modifier sits beside the wrong word.

question: A teacher chalks 'The power went out we found the candles.' on the board and lists four suggestions. Which one is not a valid fix?
answer: leave it alone -- run-ons are stylistic choices
choices: leave it alone -- run-ons are stylistic choices
add a period between clauses
add a semicolon
add a comma + coordinating conjunction
context: RUN-ONS are always errors in standard English. Standard fixes: (1) period, (2) semicolon, (3) comma + FANBOYS, (4) subordinate one clause. Stylistic run-ons in fiction ('stream of consciousness') are a separate rare exception.

question: An office memo reads, 'She wrote the letter she mailed it.' What is the best fix?
answer: 'She wrote the letter, and she mailed it.'
choices: 'She wrote the letter, and she mailed it.'
'She wrote the letter, she mailed it.'
'She wrote, the letter she mailed it.'
'She wrote the letter and, she mailed it.'
context: A comma plus AND joins the two clauses; a period or a semicolon would also work ('She wrote the letter. She mailed it.'). A bare comma makes a comma splice, and the other two put a comma where no join belongs.

question: A tutor marks two errors in one essay, writing 'comma splice' beside one line and 'run-on' beside another. What is the difference between them?
answer: splice has a comma between clauses; run-on has no punctuation at all
choices: splice has a comma between clauses; run-on has no punctuation at all
no difference
splice is worse
run-on is a comma splice with two commas
context: COMMA SPLICE = comma between full clauses ('It rained, we left'). FUSED / RUN-ON = no punctuation ('It rained we left'). Same error family, different severity.

question: A party guest's diary reads, 'The clock struck midnight everyone cheered.' Which fix keeps the two events feeling tightly linked?
answer: semicolon: 'The clock struck midnight; everyone cheered.'
choices: semicolon: 'The clock struck midnight; everyone cheered.'
period: 'The clock struck midnight. Everyone cheered.'
comma: 'The clock struck midnight, everyone cheered.'
no mark: 'The clock struck midnight everyone cheered.'
context: A semicolon joins two closely related sentences and keeps them in one breath. A period also fixes the run-on but parts the two events. A bare comma only trades the run-on for a comma splice, and no mark leaves the error as it was.

question: A boy writing about his street tries one line four ways. Which version is a run-on?
answer: The dog barked the mailman ran.
choices: The dog barked the mailman ran.
The dog barked, and the mailman ran.
The dog barked; the mailman ran.
The dog barked. The mailman ran.
context: 'The dog barked the mailman ran' has no punctuation between two full sentences, so it is fused (a run-on). The other three use standard fixes: comma + conjunction, semicolon, period.

question: A camper's journal reads, 'It was cold I put on a jacket then I went outside.' How many independent clauses are running on?
answer: three
choices: three
two
four
one
context: Each independent clause could be its own sentence: 'It was cold.' 'I put on a jacket.' 'I went outside.' All fused together = run-on. Fix: three sentences, or use punctuation between each.

question: A moving company's manual reads, "One should take the box and carry it to the kitchen." Why does that line read stiff?
answer: it uses the third person where a command would be direct
choices: it uses the third person where a command would be direct
it uses the passive voice, which hides the mover
it uses the past tense for a job still to do
it uses too many prepositions for a manual
context: Instructions want the IMPERATIVE (YOU understood). "One should" adds distance and stiffness.

question: A note on a jar reads, 'Hold the lid down, then count to ten.' Both verbs are in the imperative mood. What is the imperative mood?
answer: a verb form that gives a command
choices: a verb form that gives a command
a verb form that describes a past event
a verb form that asks a question
a verb form that states a plain fact
context: IMPERATIVE = command mood. "Close the door" means "YOU close the door" -- YOU is dropped.

question: A baker writes out step one of a cake four ways, hunting for the imperative mood, the mood of 'Turn left at the lights.' Which version uses it?
answer: Preheat the oven to 350 degrees
choices: Preheat the oven to 350 degrees
One should preheat the oven to 350 degrees
The oven should be preheated to 350 degrees
Preheating the oven is important
context: IMPERATIVE = direct command with YOU understood. The others use third person, passive, or gerund.

question: A recipe writer weighs two lines: "combine the flour and the sugar" and "one should combine the flour and the sugar." Why does the imperative win?
answer: it speaks to the cook directly; 'one should' adds distance
choices: it speaks to the cook directly; 'one should' adds distance
it uses more words than the 'one should' line
it turns the sentence into the passive voice
the 'one should' line is grammatically incorrect
context: Instructional writing wants immediacy. The imperative is direct, friendly, and clear.

question: An editor softens the order 'submit the form' into wording built on 'should' plus a verb. In which kind of writing are imperatives often replaced that way?
answer: formal academic and legal writing ("the applicant should complete section 3")
choices: formal academic and legal writing ("the applicant should complete section 3")
recipe books and cooking blogs
user manuals and assembly instructions
tutorial videos and how-to articles
context: Formal legal/academic registers sometimes soften with third-person and modal verbs. Everyday instructions use imperatives.

question: A scribe around the year 1300 wrote 'nice' in Middle English and meant something close to the opposite of its modern sense. The word came from Latin 'nescius.' What did 'nice' mean then?
answer: Foolish, silly, or ignorant
choices: Foolish, silly, or ignorant
Kind and thoughtful
Small and delicate
Wealthy and refined
context: Over roughly six centuries NICE drifted: foolish -> shy -> refined -> kind. That kind of change is called SEMANTIC SHIFT. Source: OED 'nice.'

question: A writer in the 1500s called God 'awful' and meant no insult by it. What did 'awful' mean then?
answer: Awe-inspiring and majestic
choices: Awe-inspiring and majestic
Angry and vengeful
Distant and cold
Hidden and unknowable
context: AWFUL began as awe + full: inspiring awe. Today the meaning has flipped -- AWFUL means bad, and AWESOME took over the positive sense. Source: OED 'awful.'

question: An Old English writer around the year 900 spelled 'silly' as 'saelig,' and the word meant something quite different from today. What did it mean?
answer: Blessed, happy, holy
choices: Blessed, happy, holy
Foolish or absurd
Weak and easily fooled
Loud and boisterous
context: SILLY shares a root with German 'selig' (blessed). Over centuries it drifted: blessed -> innocent -> defenseless -> foolish (by ~1600). Source: OED 'silly.'

question: A Middle English writer around 1300 called a boy a 'girl,' a word broader then than it is today. What did 'girl' mean back then?
answer: A young person of either sex
choices: A young person of either sex
A servant, either sex
A queen's attendant
A blood relative in one's own household
context: GIRL narrowed to 'young female' by the 1500s, a textbook case of semantic NARROWING -- a word whose meaning shrinks. Source: OED 'girl.'

question: A cook in Old English times called bread 'meat' and apples 'meat,' since the word meant any food. Today 'meat' means only flesh food. Which category of semantic shift is this?
answer: Narrowing -- the meaning shrank to a smaller set
choices: Narrowing -- the meaning shrank to a smaller set
Widening -- the meaning grew to a larger set
Amelioration -- the meaning became more positive
Pejoration -- the meaning became more negative
context: Any-food -> flesh-only is a smaller set: narrowing. Same shape: GIRL (any young person -> young female). Source: Grokipedia 'Semantic change' (2026-09-05).

question: A lord called his young male servant his 'cniht' in Old English, simply a boy. Centuries later a 'knight' was a noble warrior in armor. Which category of semantic shift is this?
answer: Amelioration -- the meaning became more positive
choices: Amelioration -- the meaning became more positive
Pejoration -- the meaning became more negative
Narrowing -- the meaning shrank to a smaller set
Widening -- the meaning grew to a larger set
context: Boy-servant -> noble warrior is a step up in status: amelioration. The mirror pattern is PEJORATION: VILLAIN was once just a farm worker (villein); now it means criminal. Source: Grokipedia 'Semantic change' (2026-09-05).

question: A schoolboy calls his day off a 'holiday.' The word comes from 'holy day,' and once only religious feasts counted. Which category of semantic shift is this?
answer: Widening -- the meaning grew to a larger set
choices: Widening -- the meaning grew to a larger set
Narrowing -- the meaning shrank to a smaller set
Amelioration -- the meaning became more positive
Pejoration -- the meaning became more negative
context: Holy-day-only -> any-day-off is a bigger set: widening. Same shape: DOG was originally a specific breed name; now it covers all dogs. Source: Grokipedia 'Semantic change' (2026-09-05).

question: A travel writer's bio reads, 'I have lived in Paris, France; Rome, Italy; and Athens, Greece.' Why are there semicolons between the city-country pairs instead of commas?
answer: Because each item already contains a comma; semicolons serve as super-commas to keep items distinct
choices: Because each item already contains a comma; semicolons serve as super-commas to keep items distinct
Because semicolons are more formal than commas
Because the list has exactly three items
Because English lists always use semicolons
context: When list items themselves contain commas, ordinary comma-separation blurs the boundaries. Semicolons step up as super-commas. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.60.

question: An editor stops at a line in a memoir: 'I have lived in Paris, France, Rome, Italy, and Athens, Greece.' Why is that comma-only version broken?
answer: A reader cannot tell where one item ends and the next begins
choices: A reader cannot tell where one item ends and the next begins
It has too many capital letters
It is missing an Oxford comma
The word AND should not appear before the final item
context: Ambiguity of item boundaries is exactly what super-commas solve. Rewrite as 'Paris, France; Rome, Italy; and Athens, Greece.' Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.60.

question: A teacher types up the dates for a history quiz four ways. Which version punctuates the list correctly?
answer: 'The quiz covers July 4, 1776; December 7, 1941; and September 11, 2001.'
choices: 'The quiz covers July 4, 1776; December 7, 1941; and September 11, 2001.'
'The quiz covers July 4, 1776, December 7, 1941, and September 11, 2001.'
'The quiz covers July 4, 1776: December 7, 1941: and September 11, 2001.'
'The quiz covers July 4, 1776. December 7, 1941. And September 11, 2001.'
context: Dates contain commas (July 4, 1776). Using commas between them too would blur the boundaries. Semicolons keep the three dates distinct. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.60.

question: A conference program's draft reads, 'The speakers were Dr. Alice Chen our chief scientist Mr. Ben Ortiz the operations director and Prof. Carla Vega the department head.' What is the cleanest fix?
answer: commas around each title, semicolons between the speakers
choices: commas around each title, semicolons between the speakers
commas around each title and between the speakers
colons after each name, commas between the speakers
periods between the speakers, one sentence for each
context: Each speaker's name is followed by an appositive set off with commas, so semicolons between the speakers keep the three people distinct: 'Dr. Alice Chen, our chief scientist; Mr. Ben Ortiz, the operations director; and Prof. Carla Vega, the department head.'

question: A family newsletter's draft reads, 'She invited her sister, Anna, her brother, Ben, and her mother, Carla.' What does Chicago style recommend?
answer: semicolons between items: 'her sister, Anna; her brother, Ben; and her mother, Carla'
choices: semicolons between items: 'her sister, Anna; her brother, Ben; and her mother, Carla'
colons between items: 'her sister, Anna: her brother, Ben: and her mother, Carla'
periods between items: 'her sister, Anna. Her brother, Ben. And her mother, Carla'
only commas, as written, since semicolons never separate names
context: When list items carry commas of their own (here, the commas around each name), Chicago recommends semicolons between the items so a reader sees where each one ends. Colons and periods do not separate list items, and with commas alone a reader cannot tell three people from six.

question: A tired student's essay joins two full sentences: 'It was late, however we kept working.' What punctuation does 'however' need before and after it?
answer: Semicolon BEFORE and comma AFTER: '; however,'
choices: Semicolon BEFORE and comma AFTER: '; however,'
Comma BEFORE and comma AFTER: ', however,'
Semicolon BEFORE and semicolon AFTER: '; however;'
No punctuation is needed
context: Conjunctive adverbs (however, therefore, moreover) joining two independent clauses need a SEMICOLON before and a COMMA after. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.57.

question: A night nurse's log reads, 'It was late. However we kept working.' What punctuation does 'However' take when it opens a new sentence?
answer: Just a comma AFTER: 'However, we kept working.'
choices: Just a comma AFTER: 'However, we kept working.'
A semicolon BEFORE and comma AFTER: '; However, we kept working.'
No punctuation -- it starts a sentence clean
A colon AFTER: 'However: we kept working.'
context: There is a period before, so no semicolon is needed. The sentence-initial conjunctive adverb takes only the comma after. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.57.

question: A tutor sorts connective words into three families: 'however,' 'and' and 'because.' Which note describes how each family is punctuated?
answer: 'however': semicolon before, comma after; 'and': comma before; 'because': comma when its clause leads
choices: 'however': semicolon before, comma after; 'and': comma before; 'because': comma when its clause leads
'however', 'and' and 'because': the same comma before each, nothing after
'however' and 'and': semicolon before; 'because': comma before, every time
'however': marks on both sides; 'and' and 'because': no marks at all
context: Three families, three patterns. A conjunctive adverb joining two sentences takes a semicolon before and a comma after. A coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) takes a comma before. A subordinating conjunction such as BECAUSE takes a comma when its clause opens the sentence ('Because it rained, we stayed in') and usually none when it follows. Source: Grokipedia 'Conjunctive adverb' (2026-09-05).

question: A bakery's shift report reads, 'We, however, kept working through the night.' Why does 'however' take commas there rather than a semicolon in front?
answer: HOWEVER is a MID-CLAUSE parenthetical adverb here, interrupting one clause -- commas set it off on both sides
choices: HOWEVER is a MID-CLAUSE parenthetical adverb here, interrupting one clause -- commas set it off on both sides
The sentence starts with WE -- HOWEVER never takes a semicolon after a pronoun
The sentence is a fragment -- semicolons need two independent clauses
HOWEVER always takes commas, never semicolons
context: The semicolon-before pattern is only for HOWEVER joining TWO independent clauses. Inside one clause, HOWEVER is just a parenthetical adverb, set off by commas. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.57.

question: A father writing up a road trip tries one line four ways, with 'therefore' joining two full sentences. Which version is punctuated correctly?
answer: 'The road was blocked; therefore, we took the long way home.'
choices: 'The road was blocked; therefore, we took the long way home.'
'The road was blocked, therefore we took the long way home.'
'The road was blocked, therefore, we took the long way home.'
'The road was blocked therefore we took the long way home.'
context: THEREFORE, like HOWEVER, is a conjunctive adverb. Semicolon before + comma after joins two independent clauses. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.57.

question: A weather diary reads, 'The rain stopped; the sun came out.' What is the semicolon's job there?
answer: joining two independent clauses closely related in meaning
choices: joining two independent clauses closely related in meaning
introducing a list that explains the first clause
separating the subject of a clause from its verb
marking where a quotation begins and ends
context: The semicolon's primary job: joining two independent clauses (each could be its own sentence) that are closely related. Chicago 6.56.

question: A mother fills in a school form: 'She loves reading; her sister prefers movies.' Why not use a comma there instead?
answer: a comma between two independent clauses without a conjunction is a comma splice
choices: a comma between two independent clauses without a conjunction is a comma splice
a comma would work too; the semicolon only sounds more formal
a comma would turn the second half into a sentence fragment
a comma may only separate the items of a list of three
context: Two independent clauses joined by a comma alone = comma splice (a punctuation error). Fixes: semicolon, period, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction ('She loves reading, but her sister prefers movies'). A comma does not make a fragment, and commas do far more than separate list items.

question: A short story draft reads, 'She packed her bag; and left for the airport.' What is wrong with that semicolon?
answer: 'and left for the airport' cannot stand alone as a sentence
choices: 'and left for the airport' cannot stand alone as a sentence
a semicolon must always be followed by a comma
the semicolon belongs after 'and', not before it
nothing is wrong; a semicolon may replace any comma
context: A semicolon needs a full sentence on each side, and 'and left for the airport' has no subject of its own. Drop the semicolon: 'She packed her bag and left for the airport.' One subject with two verbs needs no comma either.

question: A company's minutes read, 'The meeting was short; however, the decisions were huge.' What role does the semicolon play with the word 'however'?
answer: it joins the two clauses, since 'however' is an adverb and cannot
choices: it joins the two clauses, since 'however' is an adverb and cannot
it starts a new paragraph after the first clause
it makes the second clause depend on the first
it sets 'however' off as a one-word aside
context: 'However', 'therefore', 'moreover' and 'nevertheless' are conjunctive adverbs. They CANNOT join clauses on their own, so a semicolon (or a period) goes before them and a comma after. Chicago 6.57.

question: A hiker's postcard reads, 'The path was steep; and rocky and slippery.' What is the correct fix?
answer: drop the semicolon: 'The path was steep and rocky and slippery' (one clause)
choices: drop the semicolon: 'The path was steep and rocky and slippery' (one clause)
drop the 'and' after the semicolon
add another semicolon before 'slippery'
no fix needed
context: 'And rocky and slippery' is NOT an independent clause -- it's a list of predicate adjectives. Semicolons only join independent clauses; if only one side has a subject and verb, no semicolon.

question: A biographer's draft reads, 'She wrote the letter; because she felt she owed him a reply.' What is wrong with that line?
answer: the 'because' half cannot stand alone as a sentence
choices: the 'because' half cannot stand alone as a sentence
'because' must be followed by a comma
'letter' needs an article in front of it
the tenses of the two halves do not match
context: 'Because she felt she owed him a reply' cannot stand alone (starts with subordinating conjunction 'because'). Semicolons join TWO INDEPENDENT clauses. Fix: 'She wrote the letter because she felt...' (no punctuation).

question: A boy's note about the morning bus reads, 'Ran quickly down the street.' What is missing?
answer: the subject
choices: the subject
the verb
the object
punctuation
context: SENTENCE FRAGMENT (missing subject): a group of words with a verb but no subject cannot stand alone as a sentence. Fix by adding a subject: 'She ran quickly down the street.'

question: A postcard reads, 'Sat on the bench for hours.' A fragment is a piece of a sentence dressed up as a whole one. What kind of fragment is this?
answer: missing-subject fragment
choices: missing-subject fragment
missing-verb fragment
missing-object fragment
not a fragment
context: The verb 'sat' has no subject. Who or what sat? Fix by adding a subject: 'He sat on the bench for hours.' or 'The old cat sat on the bench for hours.'

question: A novelist tries one line four ways. Which version is a fragment because of a missing subject?
answer: Walked into the room silently.
choices: Walked into the room silently.
The tall woman walked into the room silently.
The tall woman into the room silently.
The room was entered silently.
context: 'Walked into the room silently' has no subject. Who walked? 'The tall woman into the room silently' has a subject but no verb, so it is a fragment for a different reason. The other two are complete sentences, one active and one passive.

question: A nurse's diary reads, 'Was tired after the long day.' What is the fix?
answer: 'She was tired after the long day.'
choices: 'She was tired after the long day.'
'Was tired, after the long day.'
'Was tired after the long day!'
'Tired after the long day.'
context: 'Was tired' has no subject. WHO was tired? Fix by adding one: 'She was tired after the long day.' A comma or an exclamation point changes nothing, and cutting 'was' leaves a fragment with no verb either.

question: A proud father's email reads, 'Painted the entire room in one afternoon.' What repairs that fragment?
answer: 'She painted the entire room in one afternoon.'
choices: 'She painted the entire room in one afternoon.'
'Painted the entire room, in one afternoon.'
'Painted, the entire room in one afternoon.'
'Painting the entire room in one afternoon.'
context: Add a subject to the verb 'painted': 'She painted the entire room in one afternoon.' Any noun or pronoun that could paint works (she, he, the crew). Commas do not supply a subject, and 'painting' with no helper verb is still a fragment.

question: An English teacher finds the same slip all through a stack of student stories: sentences with no subject. Why does that fragment turn up so often in writing?
answer: the subject seems obvious from context, so the writer leaves it out
choices: the subject seems obvious from context, so the writer leaves it out
the writer mistakes the verb for its own subject
the writer thinks short sentences never need one
the writer cuts it to dodge a comma splice
context: In speech and casual notes, a subject that seems obvious gets dropped ('Sat there for hours.'). Formal writing needs each sentence to carry its own subject.

question: A grandmother's journal reads, 'Went to the store yesterday. Bought bread and milk. Came home tired.' What is the issue?
answer: three fragments in a row -- each sentence lacks a subject
choices: three fragments in a row -- each sentence lacks a subject
each is a complete sentence
the tenses are wrong
commas are missing
context: The passage reads casually, but each sentence lacks a subject. Fix: 'I went to the store yesterday. I bought bread and milk. I came home tired.' Common in speech; problematic in formal writing.

question: A pet sitter's note ends, 'The huge orange cat on the windowsill.' Nothing follows. What is wrong with that as a complete sentence?
answer: It is a fragment -- no verb; the cat never does anything
choices: It is a fragment -- no verb; the cat never does anything
It has too many adjectives -- a noun may take only two
It has a comma error -- there should be a comma after CAT
It is a run-on -- two ideas jammed together
context: Every sentence needs at least a subject + verb pair. Here the subject (cat) sits alone with no verb (sat, watched, slept, jumped). Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 5.213.

question: A girl's diary reads, 'A loud crash in the kitchen at two in the morning.' What is that line called?
answer: A sentence fragment
choices: A sentence fragment
A run-on sentence
A comma splice
A subordinate clause
context: A FRAGMENT is a piece missing something it needs -- most often a verb, sometimes a subject. Source: Grokipedia 'Sentence clause structure' (2026-09-05).

question: A boy writes four lines about baking day at home. Which line is not a complete sentence?
answer: 'My grandmother's amazing chocolate chip cookies with walnuts.'
choices: 'My grandmother's amazing chocolate chip cookies with walnuts.'
'The cookies are on the counter.'
'My mother baked the cookies.'
'The cookies smell wonderful.'
context: 'My grandmother's amazing chocolate chip cookies with walnuts' is only a subject (a big noun phrase) with no verb, so it is a fragment. The other three each have a subject and a verb (are, baked, smell).

question: A children's book draft reads, 'The huge orange cat on the windowsill.' Which fix turns that into a complete sentence?
answer: 'The huge orange cat sat on the windowsill.'
choices: 'The huge orange cat sat on the windowsill.'
'The huge orange cat, on the windowsill.'
'The huge orange cat: on the windowsill.'
'The huge orange cat -- on the windowsill.'
context: Adding the verb SAT gives the subject something to do. Punctuation alone cannot fix a missing verb. Source: Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage.

question: A mystery writer's draft reads, 'In the corner of the garage behind the old bicycles under a blue tarp.' Why does that fail as a sentence even though it is long?
answer: It is a chain of prepositional phrases with no subject and no verb -- all setting, no action
choices: It is a chain of prepositional phrases with no subject and no verb -- all setting, no action
It is missing an Oxford comma
It is missing a semicolon
It has too many prepositions
context: Every phrase starts with a preposition (in, of, behind, under). None of it acts as subject or verb. Fix: give it a subject and verb -- 'We found the puzzle in the corner of the garage.' Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 5.213.

question: A tired neighbor writes four lines in a complaint to the landlord. Which line is a complete sentence?
answer: 'The dog barked all night.'
choices: 'The dog barked all night.'
'A very loud noise in the middle of the night.'
'Running down the hallway to the stairs.'
'Because the alarm went off suddenly.'
context: 'The dog barked all night' has a subject (dog) and a verb (barked). The others are a noun phrase, a participial phrase and a subordinate clause, and each is a fragment on its own.

question: A text from a friend reads, in full, 'Because it was late.' Why is that a fragment?
answer: it is a subordinate clause with no independent clause to complete the thought
choices: it is a subordinate clause with no independent clause to complete the thought
missing a subject
missing a verb
correctly punctuated
context: SUBORDINATE-CLAUSE FRAGMENT: starts with a subordinating conjunction (because, when, if, although, since, while) but has no main clause to attach to. Fix: 'Because it was late, we left.'

question: A story draft ends on the line 'When the rain finally stopped.' What is the fix?
answer: 'When the rain finally stopped, we went outside.'
choices: 'When the rain finally stopped, we went outside.'
'When the rain finally stopped; we went outside.'
'When, the rain finally stopped.'
'When the rain finally stopped!'
context: The subordinator WHEN makes the clause dependent, so it needs a main clause: 'When the rain finally stopped, we went outside.' Or drop the WHEN: 'The rain finally stopped.' A semicolon cannot attach a leaning clause, and new marks alone leave it leaning.

question: A tutor lists subordinating conjunctions, the words that can start a fragment: 'because,' 'when,' 'if' and 'although.' Which words also belong on her list?
answer: since / while / unless / until
choices: since / while / unless / until
however / therefore
and / but / or
the / a / an
context: SUBORDINATORS: because, when, if, although, since, while, unless, until, before, after, though, as. All create dependent clauses that need a main clause. CONJUNCTIVE ADVERBS (however, therefore) do not subordinate.

question: A student hands in four short lines. One holds a subject and a verb yet needs another sentence to finish it. Which line is it?
answer: Although she was tired.
choices: Although she was tired.
She was tired.
Being tired.
Very tired.
context: 'Although she was tired' is a subordinate clause (starts with ALTHOUGH). It cannot stand alone. The others: complete sentence ('She was tired'), participial fragment ('Being tired'), or adjective phrase ('Very tired').

question: A coach's text reads, 'If we leave now.' What fixes it?
answer: add a main clause: 'If we leave now, we'll catch the train.'
choices: add a main clause: 'If we leave now, we'll catch the train.'
add a semicolon: 'If we leave now; we'll catch the train.'
add a comma: 'If, we leave now.'
add an exclamation point: 'If we leave now!'
context: Two standard fixes for a subordinate-clause fragment: attach a main clause ('If we leave now, we'll catch the train.') or drop the IF ('We leave now.'). A semicolon cannot join a leaning clause to a sentence, and new marks alone leave the clause leaning.

question: A biographer opens a paragraph with 'Since he was young.' Which fix creates a complete sentence?
answer: 'Since he was young, he has loved music.'
choices: 'Since he was young, he has loved music.'
'Since he was young; he has loved music.'
'Since, he was young.'
'Since he was young, and loved music.'
context: Subordinate 'since he was young' + main clause 'he has loved music' = complete complex sentence. The subordinator needs a main clause partner to complete the thought.

question: A boy's story stops dead at 'While walking to the store.' What kind of fragment is this?
answer: a reduced subordinate clause, with no subject and no main clause
choices: a reduced subordinate clause, with no subject and no main clause
a missing-verb fragment, since 'walking' is a noun here
a run-on, since two clauses run together with no mark
a complete sentence, with 'walking' as its verb
context: 'While walking to the store' has BOTH a subordinator (while) AND no subject. Fix: 'While walking to the store, I saw an old friend' (subject in main clause) or 'While I was walking to the store, I saw an old friend'.

question: A novelist ends a chapter with 'She laughed.' What type of sentence is this?
answer: simple
choices: simple
compound
complex
compound-complex
context: SIMPLE SENTENCE = one independent clause. Subject + verb + complete thought. 'She laughed'; 'The dog barked'; 'The rain fell'. Chicago 5.219.

question: A love story's draft reads, 'She laughed, and he smiled.' What type of sentence is this?
answer: compound
choices: compound
simple
complex
fragment
context: COMPOUND SENTENCE = two or more independent clauses joined by comma+FANBOYS or a semicolon. Each clause could stand alone. 'She laughed' + 'he smiled' = two complete thoughts joined.

question: A school play's script has the line 'When she saw him, she laughed.' What type of sentence is this?
answer: complex
choices: complex
simple
compound
compound-complex
context: COMPLEX SENTENCE = one independent clause + at least one DEPENDENT clause. 'When she saw him' (dependent) + 'she laughed' (independent). Subordinators (when, because, if) create complex structure.

question: A romance writer tries out the line 'When she saw him, she laughed, and he smiled.' What type of sentence is this?
answer: compound-complex
choices: compound-complex
compound
complex
simple
context: COMPOUND-COMPLEX = at least TWO independent clauses AND at least ONE dependent clause. 'When she saw him' (dep) + 'she laughed' (indep) + 'he smiled' (indep). The most elaborate sentence type.

question: A mail carrier's complaint form reads, 'The dog barked at the mailman because it was hungry.' What type of sentence is this?
answer: complex
choices: complex
simple
compound
compound-complex
context: One independent clause ('The dog barked at the mailman') + one dependent clause ('because it was hungry'). Dependent clause introduced by BECAUSE. Complex sentence.

question: A sports page reports, 'It rained; the game was canceled.' What type of sentence is this?
answer: compound
choices: compound
simple
complex
fragment
context: Two independent clauses, each with a subject and verb, joined by a semicolon. Both could stand alone as sentences. COMPOUND -- not complex, because there is no dependent clause.

question: A fan's blog says, 'Although it rained, the game continued, and the crowd stayed loyal.' What type of sentence is this?
answer: compound-complex
choices: compound-complex
compound
complex
simple
context: 'Although it rained' (dependent) + 'the game continued' (independent) + 'the crowd stayed loyal' (independent). Two independents (compound) + one dependent (complex) = COMPOUND-COMPLEX.

question: A pet sitter's report reads, 'The cat, which had been sleeping, jumped up and ran.' What type of sentence is this?
answer: complex
choices: complex
simple
compound
fragment
context: 'The cat jumped up and ran' (independent) with 'which had been sleeping' (dependent relative clause). Compound predicate (jumped and ran) is still one clause. Result: COMPLEX sentence.

question: Gary Provost wrote a passage that runs several short sentences together, then several medium ones, one after another. What problem was he showing?
answer: strings of same-length sentences read MONOTONOUSLY -- variety creates rhythm
choices: strings of same-length sentences read MONOTONOUSLY -- variety creates rhythm
the paragraph is too short
the paragraph avoids passive voice
the paragraph uses too many commas
context: Provost's famous demonstration: same-length sentences bore the ear. Mix lengths and rhythms.

question: A writing coach hands back an essay with the words 'sentence variety' circled at the top. What rule does she mean?
answer: mix short, medium and long sentences so the rhythm keeps changing
choices: mix short, medium and long sentences so the rhythm keeps changing
use only short sentences for maximum clarity
use only long sentences to appear sophisticated
sentence variety does not affect readability
context: Variety carries the reader forward. Short for punch, medium for the main work, long for complexity.

question: An editor turns to the style guides before marking a paragraph's sentence openings. What do they advise?
answer: vary the beginnings; if every sentence starts with THE or I, the paragraph reads flat
choices: vary the beginnings; if every sentence starts with THE or I, the paragraph reads flat
always start every sentence with THE
always start every sentence with a subordinator
always start every sentence with a conjunction
context: Same-openers = monotony. Strunk & White recommend varying beginnings: phrases, clauses, conjunctions, or the subject.

question: A novelist gives her chapter three winding sentences and then this one. Snap. What technique lands the ending?
answer: a SHORT sentence after several long ones -- the contrast in length hits the reader
choices: a SHORT sentence after several long ones -- the contrast in length hits the reader
passive voice for emphasis
a subjunctive verb for uncertainty
italics on the last word
context: A short sentence after several long ones LANDS. Rhythm creates the punch.

question: An editor cuts every dead word from a paragraph and declares that it now has sentence variety. What is the truth about variety?
answer: CONCISION (cutting unnecessary words) is a separate virtue from variety
choices: CONCISION (cutting unnecessary words) is a separate virtue from variety
sentence variety is the same as concision
sentence variety is the same as passive voice
sentence variety is the same as grammar accuracy
context: Concision, clarity, voice, and variety are all separate virtues. A paragraph can vary sentences yet still be wordy.

question: A teacher counts the words in the sentences of four student paragraphs. Which paragraph has genuine sentence variety?
answer: A paragraph mixing 5-word, 15-word, and 25-word sentences
choices: A paragraph mixing 5-word, 15-word, and 25-word sentences
A paragraph of five 15-word sentences in a row
A paragraph of five 5-word sentences in a row
A paragraph of a single 60-word sentence
context: Genuine variety mixes lengths. Uniform-length paragraphs read monotonous regardless of the chosen length.

question: Cinderella's Fairy Godmother tells her, "You shall go to the ball." What does 'shall' signal there?
answer: a promise or command
choices: a promise or command
a plain future statement
a polite offer
a hypothetical statement
context: The traditional British rule: SHALL with YOU/HE/SHE/THEY signals emphasis or promise. Fairy Godmother's promise.

question: A British schoolmaster teaches the old rule for a plain future: 'shall' goes with some pronouns and not others. Which pronouns take it?
answer: I and WE
choices: I and WE
YOU only
HE, SHE and IT
YOU and THEY
context: Traditional British: I/WE take SHALL for plain futures. YOU/HE/SHE/THEY take WILL for plain futures.

question: A strict English teacher tells her class that, for emphasis, the traditional rule reverses the pronouns. Which flipped pattern is right?
answer: I WILL arrive (determined); YOU SHALL arrive (command)
choices: I WILL arrive (determined); YOU SHALL arrive (command)
I SHALL arrive (determined); YOU WILL arrive (command)
I WILL arrive (command); YOU SHALL arrive (determined)
I SHALL arrive (command); YOU WILL arrive (determined)
context: For emphasis, swap: WILL with I/WE = determined; SHALL with YOU/HE/SHE = command/promise. That is Cinderella's pattern.

question: A British visitor to the United States listens for 'shall' all week. What has become of the word in modern American English?
answer: WILL covers nearly every future; SHALL survives in law and set phrases
choices: WILL covers nearly every future; SHALL survives in law and set phrases
SHALL still pairs with I and WE, exactly as in the old British rule
SHALL has died out completely, even in contracts and statutes
SHALL marks every polite future, and WILL marks all the rest
context: SHALL has long been fading from American English. It survives in contracts ("the tenant shall pay rent") and phrases like "shall we dance?"

question: A lawyer drafting a contract writes 'shall' beside the buyer's name. What does the word usually mean there?
answer: "is required to" -- a mandatory duty
choices: "is required to" -- a mandatory duty
"is allowed to" -- a permission
"will probably" -- a future statement
"hopes to" -- an aspiration
context: Legal SHALL = mandatory. Lawyers debate replacing every SHALL with MUST or WILL to remove ambiguity.

question: A gatekeeper bars the road and hands down an order in the old emphatic style. Which line fits the traditional rule?
answer: You shall not pass!
choices: You shall not pass!
You will not pass!
You may not pass!
You could not pass!
context: Gandalf on the bridge: SHALL with YOU for emphasis/command. Classic traditional pattern.

question: A text to a sister reads, 'I should of gone.' What is wrong with that sentence?
answer: 'of' should be 'have'
choices: 'of' should be 'have'
'should' should be 'would'
'gone' should be 'went'
nothing is wrong
context: 'Should've' (contraction of 'should have') SOUNDS identical to 'should of' when spoken -- but 'of' is a preposition and cannot follow modal verbs. Written correctly: 'should have' or 'should've'.

question: A track coach's email says, 'She could of won that race.' What is the correct written form?
answer: could have
choices: could have
could of
could had
coulda
context: 'Could've' → 'could of' is the classic mishearing. Modal verbs (should, would, could, might, must, may) take 'have' + past participle. 'Have' contracts to 've, which sounds like 'of'.

question: A boy writes 'should of' in his essay and swears it sounds right. Why does it sound right to so many speakers?
answer: the contraction 'should've' sounds just like 'should of'
choices: the contraction 'should've' sounds just like 'should of'
'of' once served as a helping verb in older English
'should of' is the standard form in British English
it copies the pattern of phrases like 'kind of'
context: The reduced schwa sound of contracted 'have' (should've = /ʃʊdəv/) is identical to unstressed 'of' (/əv/). The ear hears them the same. Only writing exposes the mistake.

question: A tutor lists the modal verbs 'should,' 'could,' 'would' and 'might' on a card. Which word follows them in the perfect tense?
answer: have
choices: have
of
had
did
context: Modal + HAVE + past participle = modal perfect. 'Should have gone' (regret), 'could have won' (past possibility), 'would have called' (unreal past). Never modal + OF.

question: A mother's text reads, 'she must of forgotten.' What is the correct written form of 'must of'?
answer: 'must have'
choices: 'must have'
'must of'
'must has'
'must had'
context: 'Must've' = 'must have'. Same mishearing pattern -- the reduced 've' contraction sounds identical to 'of'. Applies to all modals: should, would, could, might, must, may.

question: A teenager texts back, 'I would of if I could of.' How many corrections does that sentence need?
answer: two
choices: two
one
three
none
context: BOTH modal auxiliaries are wrong. Every 'of' after a modal (should, would, could, might, must, may) is a mishearing of 'have' or 've. Both need correction.

question: A school essay reads, 'She should have of thought twice.' What is the correct form?
answer: 'She should have thought twice.'
choices: 'She should have thought twice.'
'She should of thought twice.'
'She should've of thought twice.'
'She should had thought twice.'
context: Modal (should) + HAVE + past participle (thought). 'Of' has no job after 'have', so it comes out. 'Should've of' adds the same slip to a contraction, and 'should had' uses the wrong form of 'have'.

question: A novelist writes 'should of' into a line of dialogue, and her editor leaves it in. Why is that acceptable?
answer: the dialogue spells out how the character really talks
choices: the dialogue spells out how the character really talks
'of' has become an accepted helping verb after modals
novels are exempt from the rules of standard English
editors now treat 'should of' as a correct spelling
context: Eye-dialect: fiction writers spell nonstandard speech phonetically ('should of', 'coulda', 'gonna') to signal a character's register. Legitimate device inside quoted speech; not acceptable in the narrator's voice.

question: A reporter at an American newspaper quotes a man who is repeating another man's words. Which quote marks wrap the outer quote and which the inner?
answer: DOUBLE outer, SINGLE inner: "She said, ‘hello.’"
choices: DOUBLE outer, SINGLE inner: "She said, ‘hello.’"
SINGLE outer, DOUBLE inner: ‘She said, "hello."’
both use double quotes
both use single quotes
context: American convention: outer double, inner single. British historically the reverse (modern British varies).

question: A book editor of the old school marks up a quotation inside a quotation. In traditional British style, which quote marks are outer and which are inner?
answer: SINGLE outer, DOUBLE inner (though modern British usage varies)
choices: SINGLE outer, DOUBLE inner (though modern British usage varies)
DOUBLE outer, SINGLE inner (American style)
always double
always single
context: Historical British: reverse of American. Oxford now allows either as house style. Modern practice varies.

question: An American court reporter types a quotation inside a quotation inside a quotation. What is the pattern of marks, from outer to innermost?
answer: double, single, double (alternating)
choices: double, single, double (alternating)
single, double, single (British reverse)
all single all the way
all double all the way
context: Alternate marks with each level of nesting. American pattern starts with double; British reverse pattern starts with single.

question: A columnist uses scare quotes in his review of a rival's book. What are scare quotes?
answer: quotes around a word to show the writer doubts or mocks it
choices: quotes around a word to show the writer doubts or mocks it
quotes around a word the writer wants to stress
quotes that mark a speaker's exact words
quotes required around every technical term
context: Scare quotes signal skepticism or ironic distance: his "research" turned out to be three websites. They do not add emphasis; a word put in quotation marks for stress reads as doubt instead. American writers usually use double marks for them.

question: A proofreader looks up the single quote mark in his style sheet and reads where specialists use it on purpose. Which field or fields does the sheet name?
answer: linguistics (word meanings) and botany (cultivar names)
choices: linguistics (word meanings) and botany (cultivar names)
law (contract clauses) and medicine (drug names)
poetry (line breaks) and drama (stage directions)
chemistry (formulas) and music (key signatures)
context: Linguists put a word's meaning in single quotes: Latin canis ‘dog’. Gardeners and botanists put the name of a cultivated variety in single quotes: Rosa ‘Peace’. Domain-specific conventions.

question: A sign at King Arthur's Round Table reads: 'Each knight sits in ___ seat.' Which word keeps all the knights from piling into one chair?
answer: his
choices: his
their
its
theirs
context: EACH KNIGHT means one knight at a time, so the pronoun is singular: 'Each knight sits in his seat.' THEIR would give the whole fellowship one seat to share. ITS is for things and animals, and THEIRS stands alone ('the seats are theirs'), never before a noun.

question: A bus driver's note reads, '___ forgot his own lunch on the bus.' Which word can open that sentence?
answer: Everybody
choices: Everybody
Both
Several
Many
context: EVERYBODY -- like everyone, anyone and nobody -- is grammatically SINGULAR, so it takes HIS: 'Everybody forgot his own lunch on the bus.' BOTH, SEVERAL and MANY are always plural and would need THEIR: 'Many forgot their own lunches.' A handy check: 'everybody IS,' but 'many ARE.'

question: A note left by the phone says, 'If anyone calls, tell ___ I'll be back at noon.' Which word belongs in the blank?
answer: him
choices: him
them
he
his
context: ANYONE points to one caller, so the pronoun is singular. After the verb TELL, the pronoun is an object, so it takes the object form HIM: 'If anyone calls, tell him I'll be back at noon.' HE is the subject form, and HIS shows ownership. THEM is plural and would turn one caller into a crowd.

question: A proctor's exam instructions read, 'Each student should check his or her answers before he or she hands in his or her test.' Which revision keeps the agreement and loses the clutter?
answer: Students should check their answers before they hand in their tests.
choices: Students should check their answers before they hand in their tests.
Students should check his answers before he hands in his tests.
Students should check their answers before they hands in their tests.
Students should check his or her answers before they hand in their tests.
context: Three HIS OR HERs and a HE OR SHE in one sentence are correct but clumsy. The cleanest fix makes the subject plural, so every pronoun can be plural too: 'Students should check their answers before they hand in their tests.' Plain HIS also works with a singular subject: 'Each student should check his answers before he hands in his test.' Use HIS OR HER sparingly -- once, not three times.

question: A coach's season report reads, 'After the big game, everyone on the team was proud of ___.' Which word belongs in the blank?
answer: himself
choices: himself
themselves
hisself
itself
context: A REFLEXIVE pronoun (one ending in -SELF) points back to the subject. The subject here is EVERYONE, which is singular, so the reflexive is singular too: 'Everyone on the team was proud of himself.' HISSELF is a dialect form that standard English does not use, and ITSELF is for things and animals. To praise the whole squad at once, go plural: 'The players were proud of themselves.'

question: A ship's log reads, 'Neither the sailors nor the captain could find ___ compass.' Which pronoun belongs in the blank?
answer: his
choices: his
their
its
theirs
context: When two subjects are joined by OR or NOR, the pronoun agrees with the NEARER one. The captain stands next to the blank and is one man, so HIS: 'Neither the sailors nor the captain could find his compass.' Flip the order and the plural wins: 'Neither the captain nor the sailors could find their compass.' Many writers put the plural last for exactly that reason -- it sounds smoother.

question: A school handbook reads, 'A student should bring ___ book to class.' Traditional grammar puts 'his' in the blank. Why is 'his' right?
answer: A STUDENT is one person, and a pronoun matches the noun it points back to
choices: A STUDENT is one person, and a pronoun matches the noun it points back to
BOOK is singular, and a pronoun matches the noun that comes after it
HIS is the only pronoun short enough to sit in front of a noun
CLASS is singular, so every pronoun in the sentence must be singular
context: A pronoun agrees with its ANTECEDENT -- the noun it refers back to -- not with whatever noun comes next. Here the antecedent is A STUDENT: one person, so one singular pronoun. By long tradition HIS covers a student of either sex; William Strunk's 1918 guide 'The Elements of Style' told writers to use HE after words like 'each' and 'everybody' unless the person is or must be female. To skip the question entirely, go plural: 'Students should bring their books to class.'

question: A substitute teacher hands her class four rules of writing. Three are schoolroom superstitions that good writers break all the time. Which one is a real rule of standard English?
answer: A pronoun must agree in number with the word it refers to
choices: A pronoun must agree in number with the word it refers to
Never split an infinitive, as in 'to boldly go'
Never end a sentence with a preposition
Never begin a sentence with 'And' or 'But'
context: Pronoun agreement is the real rule: a singular word like EVERYONE or EACH STUDENT takes a singular pronoun ('Everyone did his part'), and a plural word takes a plural one ('All the students did their parts'). The other three were never rules of English grammar at all. They were borrowed from Latin or invented as classroom habits, and good writers from Shakespeare to the makers of Star Trek have broken them freely.

question: A school form asks for the signature of 'the parent and/or guardian.' What does the slash indicate?
answer: alternatives or both (either-or plus both)
choices: alternatives or both (either-or plus both)
a fraction
a date separator
a division sign
context: AND/OR slash: indicates "either-or, or both together." Chicago dislikes it and prefers recasting the sentence.

question: An American museum label reads "7/4/1776." What does that date mean in US convention?
answer: month/day/year -- July 4, 1776
choices: month/day/year -- July 4, 1776
day/month/year -- April 7, 1776
year/month/day -- ISO format
a fraction
context: US slash-date: MM/DD/YYYY. UK: DD/MM/YYYY. Real communication hazard when the number could be a month or a day.

question: A programmer labels her files under the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 8601 date standard. What order does that format use for year, month and day?
answer: YYYY-MM-DD (largest unit first, with hyphens)
choices: YYYY-MM-DD (largest unit first, with hyphens)
MM/DD/YYYY (US slash format)
DD/MM/YYYY (UK slash format)
DD-MON-YYYY (day-month-name-year)
context: ISO 8601 = international standard. Year first, then month, then day, with hyphens. Sortable and unambiguous.

question: A student's essay quotes poetry in the middle of a paragraph: 'Two roads diverged in a yellow wood, / And sorry I could not travel both.' What does the slash mark?
answer: line breaks in the original poem, with space before and after
choices: line breaks in the original poem, with space before and after
stanza breaks
author attribution
a false start
context: Slash marks line breaks in cited poetry. Example: "Whose woods these are I think I know / His house is in the village though." Space before AND after.

question: An old Oxford story credits Reverend Spooner with the line "You have tasted the whole worm." What did he mean to say?
answer: WASTED THE WHOLE TERM (the opening consonants of two words are swapped)
choices: WASTED THE WHOLE TERM (the opening consonants of two words are swapped)
TESTED THE OLD FIRM (a different swap)
ATE THE ENTIRE MEAL (a different meaning)
the phrase was correct as spoken
context: Classic Spooner slip: swap T and W. WASTED THE TERM -> TASTED THE WORM. Names the pattern.

question: A man consoles a neighbor over 'a blushing crow' when he means 'a crushing blow.' That line is a spoonerism. What is a spoonerism?
answer: a slip in which the opening consonants (or syllables) of two words are exchanged
choices: a slip in which the opening consonants (or syllables) of two words are exchanged
a word that reads the same forward and backward
a word that combines two others into one
a rhetorical figure using a single verb for two objects
context: Named after Rev. William Archibald Spooner (1844-1930), Warden of New College, Oxford. He reportedly produced many; most attributed to him are apocryphal.

question: A delighted student repeats a line attributed to Reverend Spooner: "You have hissed all my mystery lectures." What did Spooner mean to say?
answer: MISSED all my HISTORY lectures
choices: MISSED all my HISTORY lectures
HIT all my MASTERY lectures
FINISHED all my MEMORY lectures
the phrase was correct as spoken
context: H and M swap: HISSED MYSTERY -> MISSED HISTORY. Same pattern as the "tasted the worm" line.

question: An Oxford tour guide repeats a spoonerism as Reverend Spooner's own words. What caveat should a careful listener add?
answer: most lines credited to him were made up by others
choices: most lines credited to him were made up by others
every line credited to him is on record
he wrote the lines down himself as jokes
he never existed; he is an Oxford legend
context: Historians confirm only a small number of authentic Spooner slips. The rest are later inventions attached to his name.

question: A comedian trots out an old bar joke: "I'd rather have a bottle in front of me than a frontal lobotomy." What makes that line a joke?
answer: it uses a spoonerism (swapped sounds)
choices: it uses a spoonerism (swapped sounds)
it uses zeugma (one verb, two objects)
it uses anaphora (repeated opening)
it uses hyperbole (exaggeration)
context: 'Bottle in front' and 'frontal lobotomy' carry the same two sounds in reverse order, BOT then FRONT and then FRONT then BOT, so a drinker's line doubles as a medical one. That deliberate swap is a spoonerism played for laughs. Zeugma hangs one verb on two objects, anaphora repeats an opening, and hyperbole exaggerates; the line does none of those.

question: A class note reads, 'The teacher told the class often to study for the quiz.' Was the telling often, or the studying? What is that kind of adverb called?
answer: A squinting modifier
choices: A squinting modifier
A misplaced modifier
A dangling modifier
A subordinating conjunction
context: SQUINTING: the adverb sits between two verbs and could modify either. Named because it looks both ways. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 5.171.

question: A teacher circles one adverb in a student's draft: it could belong to either of two nearby verbs. What is the fix?
answer: Move the adverb next to the verb it should modify
choices: Move the adverb next to the verb it should modify
Set the adverb off with a comma on each side
Swap the adverb for a stronger synonym
Turn the adverb into an adjective
context: Placement is the whole cure. 'The teacher OFTEN told the class to study' fixes one reading; 'The teacher told the class to study OFTEN' fixes the other. Source: Fowler's Modern English Usage, 'squinting adverbs.'

question: A school flyer promises, 'Students who study rarely fail the test.' What is the problem with that promise?
answer: RARELY is ambiguous -- it could go with STUDY or FAIL
choices: RARELY is ambiguous -- it could go with STUDY or FAIL
STUDENTS needs an apostrophe -- it is possessive
WHO should be WHOM -- it is the verb's object
STUDY should be STUDIES -- the subject is singular
context: RARELY sits between STUDY and FAIL -- either verb could take it. Moving it fixes the promise: 'Students who rarely study fail' or 'Students who study fail rarely.' Source: Grokipedia 'Squinting modifier' (2026-09-05).

question: A gym's poster reads, 'The people who exercise regularly stay healthy.' Which two readings does its adverb allow?
answer: they work out often, or they stay well as a rule
choices: they work out often, or they stay well as a rule
they work out often, or they work out hard
they are ordinary people, or they work out often
they work out often, or they eat healthy food
context: REGULARLY sits between EXERCISE and STAY. It could modify either. Moving it next to the verb the writer means settles the reading.

question: A grammar teacher writes 'squinting,' 'misplaced' and 'dangling' on the board as three related modifier bugs. How do they differ?
answer: SQUINTING has two possible owners; MISPLACED, the wrong owner; DANGLING, none
choices: SQUINTING has two possible owners; MISPLACED, the wrong owner; DANGLING, none
SQUINTING has no owner; MISPLACED, two possible owners; DANGLING, the wrong owner
SQUINTING has the wrong owner; MISPLACED, no owner; DANGLING, two possible owners
SQUINTING has two possible owners; MISPLACED, no owner; DANGLING, the wrong owner
context: 'Walking to school, the trees were beautiful' = DANGLING (who is walking?). 'I saw a horse riding to school' = MISPLACED (the horse is not riding). 'Students who study rarely fail' = SQUINTING (RARELY between STUDY and FAIL). Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e sections 5.171-5.173.

question: A tutor pins up four student sentences and asks for the modifier that could belong to either of two nearby verbs. Which sentence holds it?
answer: 'The coach said after the game the team would practice.'
choices: 'The coach said after the game the team would practice.'
'Walking to school, the trees were beautiful.'
'I saw a horse riding down the street.'
'She had a picture of her dog on her desk.'
context: 'After the game' squints between SAID (said after the game) and WOULD PRACTICE (practice after the game). The trees sentence is DANGLING; the horse sentence is MISPLACED; the dog-picture sentence is ambiguous too (is the dog or the picture on the desk?), but it has only one verb, so nothing in it can squint between two verbs.

question: A nurse's note reads, 'The doctor said in the morning the patient would feel better.' Which two readings does 'in the morning' allow, and what is the fix?
answer: the saying or the recovery -- move the phrase beside one verb
choices: the saying or the recovery -- move the phrase beside one verb
the saying or the recovery -- set the phrase off with commas
the doctor or the patient -- swap the two nouns around
only the recovery -- the sentence needs no fix at all
context: The phrase can modify either verb, the saying or the feeling better; placement settles it. Move it before SAID or after BETTER. Commas leave both readings standing.

question: A note to a friend reads, "I bought some stationary for my thank-you cards." Which word was misused?
answer: "stationary" (should be "stationery")
choices: "stationary" (should be "stationery")
"bought" (should be "brought")
"cards" (should be "card's")
"some" (should be "sum")
context: STATIONERY (with -ery) = writing paper. STATIONARY (with -ary) = not moving. Cards need paper.

question: A store's price list offers 'a stationary bicycle.' What does that mean?
answer: a bike that doesn't move
choices: a bike that doesn't move
a bike with a single fixed gear
a bike sold at a stationery shop
a bike built for delivering mail
context: STATIONARY = still, not moving. Gym bike stays in one place.

question: A teacher chalks 'stationary' beside its -ery look-alike and gives her class one note to keep the spellings apart. What does it say?
answer: stationERy has E like Envelope; stationARy has A like stAy
choices: stationERy has E like Envelope; stationARy has A like stAy
stationARy has A like pAper; stationERy has E like stEady
stationERy has E like stEady; stationARy has A like cArd
stationARy has A like mAil; stationERy has E like rEst
context: E for envelope/letter; A for stAy. The single letter shows which meaning applies.

question: A note on an office desk reads, "The ___ is in the drawer." Which spelling means the writing paper is stored there?
answer: stationery
choices: stationery
stationary
stationer
station
context: STATIONERY = paper, envelopes, pens. The drawer holds writing supplies. A STATIONER is the person who sells them, and a STATION is a standing place.

question: An editor checks four sentences that all use the word 'stationary.' In which one is the word used correctly?
answer: The old grandfather clock stood stationary in the corner
choices: The old grandfather clock stood stationary in the corner
He ordered engraved stationary for the wedding invitations
She keeps stationary in the top drawer of her desk
The bookshop sells stationary and greeting cards
context: STATIONARY (not moving) fits the clock. The other three describe paper goods and need STATIONERY.

question: A student finds 'stationary' beside its look-alike in a dictionary. Why did the two spellings split?
answer: medieval booksellers kept fixed STATIONS, so their goods became STATIONERY
choices: medieval booksellers kept fixed STATIONS, so their goods became STATIONERY
the paper word came from French and the standing word from Latin
the E came from a printer's error in an early dictionary
they are not actually related; the shared root is coincidence
context: Medieval booksellers, unlike traveling peddlers, kept fixed stations, often near a university, and were called stationers. By the early 1700s their goods were called stationery, and the -ERY spelling came to mark the paper trade.

question: A neighbor's note reads, 'The dog ___ barking.' Which verb form fits?
answer: is
choices: is
are
were
am
context: SUBJECT-VERB AGREEMENT: singular subjects take singular verbs, plural subjects take plural verbs. The dog IS. The dogs ARE. Chicago 5.140.

question: A boy texts from the yard, 'The dogs ___ barking.' Which verb form fits?
answer: are
choices: are
is
was
am
context: Plural subject → plural verb. Two dogs bark; they ARE barking. The verb form must match the true subject's number.

question: A mother frowns at a shopping note: 'The list of items ___ long.' Which verb form fits?
answer: is
choices: is
are
were
seem
context: PREPOSITIONAL PHRASES DO NOT DETERMINE THE VERB. The subject is LIST (singular), not ITEMS. Common trap: the nearest noun is not always the subject.

question: A florist proofs four lines for her shop's flyer. Which line has a subject-verb agreement error?
answer: The bouquet of flowers were beautiful.
choices: The bouquet of flowers were beautiful.
The bouquet of flowers was beautiful.
The flowers in the bouquet were beautiful.
The flowers, in a bouquet, were beautiful.
context: Subject = BOUQUET (singular). The prepositional phrase 'of flowers' does not make it plural. Correct: 'The bouquet was beautiful.' The plural attractor 'flowers' is the trap.

question: A first-grade worksheet reads, 'Two plus two ___ four.' Which verb do most usage guides prefer?
answer: is
choices: is
are
were
am
context: Most usage guides prefer the singular for arithmetic, since the sum is one thing, though some accept 'two plus two are four' too. 'Ten divided by five is two.' Same idea: 'Twenty dollars is a lot of money' (an amount, one unit).

question: A boy haggling at a yard sale says, 'Ten dollars ___ enough.' Which verb fits?
answer: is
choices: is
are
were
seem
context: MONEY, TIME, DISTANCE amounts take singular verbs when treated as one quantity. 'Ten dollars is enough'; 'five miles is a long walk'; 'three hours is not enough time'.

question: A project report reads, 'One of the reasons the plan failed ___ funding.' Which verb fits?
answer: was
choices: was
were
are
have been
context: The subject is ONE (singular). 'Of the reasons' is a prepositional phrase. 'The plan failed' is a relative clause modifying 'reasons'. The main verb agrees with ONE → was.

question: An older sister's note says, 'If I ___ you, I would apologise.' Which verb form does traditional grammar require?
answer: were
choices: were
was
am
will be
context: The SUBJUNCTIVE MOOD is used for hypothetical, counter-to-fact, or wished-for statements. 'If I WERE you' -- I am not you, so 'were' (subjunctive), not 'was' (indicative). Chicago 5.128.

question: A tutor tells a student that the subjunctive is the mood for what is not so. After what starter phrases does it show up?
answer: 'if... were' and 'I wish... were'
choices: 'if... were' and 'I wish... were'
'because... was' and 'since... was'
'when... is' and 'while... is'
'after... will be' and 'before... will be'
context: Subjunctive triggers: IF (contrary to fact) and WISH take WERE for every subject, and AS IF and SUPPOSE can take it too. Demands take the bare form: 'I insist that he BE present.' BECAUSE, WHEN and AFTER report real events in the indicative.

question: A camp counselor's note reads, 'If it ___ raining, we would stay inside.' Which verb form fits in standard written English?
answer: were
choices: were
was
is
will be
context: Counter-to-fact conditional ('if it were raining' but it isn't). WERE is the subjunctive form regardless of the subject's number: 'if I were', 'if he were', 'if she were', 'if it were'.

question: A school principal writes, 'I insist that she ___ present.' Which verb form belongs there in formal English?
answer: be
choices: be
is
was
were
context: MANDATIVE SUBJUNCTIVE: after verbs of demand, request, suggestion, or requirement, the following verb takes the bare infinitive (be, arrive, submit). 'I demand that he BE quiet'; 'I suggest that she GO'.

question: A student's short story reads, "She said that she IS tired." What is the standard reported-speech rule?
answer: after a past reporting verb, the inner verb shifts back: IS becomes WAS
choices: after a past reporting verb, the inner verb shifts back: IS becomes WAS
reported speech always keeps the original present tense
reported speech always uses future tense
reported speech drops the "that" and keeps everything else
context: Past reporting verb triggers backshift. IS becomes WAS.

question: A teacher opens a grammar lesson by pointing to the words "reported speech" on her slide. What does the term mean?
answer: retelling what a person said without quoting the exact words
choices: retelling what a person said without quoting the exact words
quoting a person word for word inside quotation marks
writing in the first person about one's own thoughts
a style of journalism built on interview transcripts
context: Reported speech = indirect discourse. Removes the quotation marks and shifts tense to match the reporting verb.

question: "I am leaving tomorrow," a boy tells his aunt, and later she passes his words on, starting with "He said..." What does "am" become?
answer: past (was)
choices: past (was)
future (will be)
past perfect (had been)
present perfect (has been)
context: The backshift rule: PRESENT -> PAST when reporting from a past viewpoint.

question: A news reporter turns a quote into reported speech after "She said that..." and comes to the past verb "was." What does "was" become?
answer: past perfect (had been)
choices: past perfect (had been)
present (is)
future (will be)
past continuous (was being)
context: PAST -> PAST PERFECT. The backshift goes one further step back.

question: A boy repeats a friend's promise to his mother: "She said, ‘I will call you.’" How does he put it into reported speech?
answer: She said she WOULD call me
choices: She said she WOULD call me
She said she WOULD HAVE called me
She said she CALLS me
She said she is calling me
context: WILL shifts to WOULD in reported speech. Modal verbs also backshift: CAN->COULD, MAY->MIGHT, WILL->WOULD. ('She said she will call me' can stand if the call is still to come.)
